newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko tells West not to push Belarus around.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko tells West not to push Belarus around.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko insisted on Tuesday that Belarus was a reliable partner in the quest for world security but warned the West not to push it around.

Lukashenko and visiting Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov also restated their firm opposition to NATO expansion, with Primakov resurrecting the tough rhetoric which caused jitters before a Russia-U.S. summit in Helsinki last month.
"We consider NATO expansion to be the biggest mistake since the end of the Cold War," Primakov said, repeating a phrase used by Russian President Boris Yeltsin on the eve of the summit.
Yeltsin softened his tone after the meeting with President Bill Clinton, in which the two men "agreed to disagree" on the expansion issue.

Speaking at a conference in Minsk dedicated to the idea of creating a nuclear-free central Europe, Lukashenko said he was complaining loudly about NATO's expansion plans because they would create a new dividing line right on his doorstep.
"Unfortunately, today we are forced to state...that certain parts of the military infrastructure of NATO are moving towards the Belarussian borders," he said, without elaborating.

NATO does not plan to start the long process of expansion until July, when the first new members from eastern Europe are expected to be invited in. They are set to include Poland, which shares a border with Belarus.

Both Russia and Belarus, which are planning to integrate, argue that NATO expansion threatens their security and dismiss the West's argument that the western defence alliance is not directed against their states. But they also accept that NATO is unlikely to change its plans.
Primakov and Lukashenko told reporters they had put the final touches to a charter on integrating their two states.
The charter, initialled by Lukashenko and Yeltsin last week, will now be published for discussion by people in both countries over the next month.

Primakov said Belarus' initiative to create a nuclear-free zone in central Europe could become one of the elements of the new European security struture, which is expected to include a bilateral deal between NATO and Russia.
Lukashenko said Belarus also sought a judicial guarantee of its security if NATO expansion went ahead.

"We also intend to further broaden and deepen cooperation with the European Union, other European structures in all areas, including the issue of fulfilling the OSCE's rules in the human dimension," he said, clearly using a euphemism for human rights.
"But problems here must be resolved on the basis of equal dialogue and not through pressure or interference in our internal affairs."

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) last year criticised a referendum in Belarus in which Lukashenko ignored other branches of power and the old constitution to push through a poll on expanding his powers, which he won by a landslide.
A Council of Europe analysis of the new constitution says it concentrates nearly all power in the president's hands and poses a real threat to democracy and human rights.
Lukashenko, who is popular in Belarus, argues that his people simply have a different vision on these issues and accuses the opposition and foreign journalists of bias.
